question: How does the Python GIL affect CPU-bound multithreaded programs?
report_draft: In standard CPython, the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) restricts execution so that only one thread can run Python bytecode at a time [c:t3-r1-c1]. This limitation means that parallel CPU execution is constrained when using multithreading [c:t3-r1-c6]. Consequently, the GIL prevents true parallelism in CPU-bound multithreaded programs, resulting in performance that is similar to or slightly slower than single-threaded execution [c:t1-r1-c5]. Because of this, multithreading is generally not suitable for speeding up CPU-bound Python code [c:t3-r1-c2]. Although CPython periodically releases the GIL to allow other threads to execute, with a default switch interval of 5 milliseconds that is tunable via sys.setswitchinterval(), this does not enable true parallelism for CPU-bound tasks [c:t1-r1-c3]. Instead, multiprocessing is best suited for CPU-bound tasks, whereas multithreading is best suited for I/O-bound tasks [c:t3-r1-c5]. Multiprocessing allows for true parallel execution of CPU-bound workloads because separate processes can run on different CPU cores [c:t3-r1-c3]. In a multiprocessing setup, each process has its own GIL, allowing work to be distributed across multiple processes [c:t3-r1-c4].
